questions.question: Does a capacitor store charge or energy? Be precise.
questions.solution: Strictly, it stores ENERGY (½CV²) in the electric field between the plates; the NET charge added is zero — the two plates hold +Q and −Q, equal and opposite. 'Storing charge' is loose language for separating charge. The field between the plates is where the energy actually sits.

questions.question: Why does inserting a dielectric between the plates increase capacitance?
questions.solution: The dielectric's molecules polarise: their induced/surface charges create an internal field opposing the applied one, reducing the net field by factor K (dielectric constant). Lower field for the same free charge means lower potential difference — and C = Q/V rises by factor K. The dielectric weakens the field the plates' charges create.

questions.question: Capacitors combine oppositely to resistors: series capacitors give LESS capacitance, parallel give MORE. Explain both with the physics.
questions.solution: Parallel: all plates share the same V, charges add — Q = (C₁+C₂)V, so capacitances ADD (more plate area effectively). Series: the same charge Q flows through each (induced charges), voltages add — V = Q(1/C₁ + 1/C₂), so 1/C_total = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ and the combination is smaller than the smallest. Voltage divides in series; charge adds in parallel.

questions.question: A capacitor charged by a battery then DISCONNECTED: what happens to its energy if you pull the plates apart? What if the battery stays connected?
questions.solution: Disconnected: Q is fixed; pulling apart increases V (= Q/C, C falls), so U = Q²/2C RISES — you do work against the attraction. Connected: V is fixed by the battery; C falls, Q = CV falls, and U = ½CV² FALLS — the extra energy returns to the battery. Which quantity is held fixed decides the answer.

questions.question: Why does a capacitor pass no steady current in a DC circuit but appear to 'pass' AC?
questions.solution: Charge can only accumulate on the plates, not cross the gap: once V_capacitor = V_source, current stops — DC is blocked after the transient. AC keeps reversing polarity, so the plates charge and discharge each half-cycle — current flows in the wires continuously even though no charge crosses the dielectric. The plates' changing charge IS the 'current through' the capacitor.

questions.question: Sliding a plastic slab between the plates of an isolated charged capacitor increases its capacitance. Where does the extra energy come from?
questions.solution: The dielectric polarises: its dipoles align against the field and produce a counter-field, so the voltage across the plates falls while charge Q is unchanged. Since C = Q/V, a smaller V means larger C. The stored energy ½QV actually DECREASES, and the difference is the mechanical work the slab does as it is pulled in. The dielectric is drawn into the gap by the field.

questions.concept: Series and parallel the other way round
questions.question: Capacitors combine the OPPOSITE way to resistors: parallel adds capacitances, series gives a smaller value. Why the reversal?
questions.solution: Resistors in series share the same CURRENT and voltages add; capacitors in parallel share the same VOLTAGE and charges add (Q = Q₁+Q₂), giving C = C₁+C₂. In series capacitors carry the same charge and their voltages add, so 1/C = Σ1/Cᵢ yields a smaller effective C. The rules follow which quantity is common, and that is inverted between the two devices. Study the shared quantity, not the formula.

questions.concept: Why a capacitor blocks DC but passes AC
questions.question: A capacitor in series with a lamp: nothing with DC, but the lamp glows with AC. Why?
questions.solution: DC cannot cross the insulating gap, so once charged, no steady current flows. AC keeps reversing, so the capacitor charges, discharges and recharges continuously — charge sloshes back and forth through the external circuit, which IS a current, though no charge crosses the dielectric. A capacitor passes changes, not steady flow: it is a differentiator, not a wire.
